World.title: Football Australia to slash 20 per cent of workforce as CEO makes damning admission
World.content:
SportSoccerAustralian soccer Football Australia to slash 20 per cent of workforce as CEO makes damning admission Vince Rugari May 19, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Football Australia is bracing for another massive financial loss, triggering a sweeping internal restructure that will see it shed over 20 per cent of its workforce – and an admission from chief executive Martin Kugeler that the game has failed to harness the rise of the Matildas and the success of a home World Cup in 2023. Having posted a record $8.5 million deficit in last year’s accounts, worse numbers will be revealed at FA’s annual general meeting next Thursday as Kugeler confronts the organisation’s financial reality. Loading Kugeler would not speak to specifics of the latest loss, other than to say it was “more significant” than the last. “We are not where we need to be on the financial side,” Kugeler said on Tuesday. “And that’s what we have to address. We have to live with our means. We have to establish an organisation and a structure that will support taking advantage of the opportunities that we have ahead.”



FA would not confirm its headcount, but sources not authorised to comment publicly due to the sensitivity of the situation, suggest it is fewer than 200 people. Whatever the figure, the prospective loss of at least one in five workers follows a “right-sizing” effort after the 2025 AGM, which suggests the initial cuts did not go far enough. It comes less than three years after Australia co-hosted the FIFA Women’s World Cup and weeks after the conclusion of the AFC Women’s Asian Cup, two major tournaments that were supposed to usher the sport – and FA – into an era of commercial prosperity. Sam Kerr during the Women’s Asian Cup. Getty Images Instead, despite record participation numbers and the emergence of the Matildas as a premium national sporting brand, both FA and the Australian Professional Leagues, the body which runs the A-Leagues, have been forced into dramatic cost-cutting exercises to stay afloat. In good news, FA and the APL have reached a settlement over historic debts between the two organisations, relating to product betting fees from gambling companies and refereeing expenses. The last AGM was clouded by confusion over the nature of FA’s $8.5 million loss, with $4.1 million attributed to expected credit losses, which sources at the time said was due to debts from the APL that FA was not anticipating would be paid.



The resolution of those issues at least gives Kugeler a more solid domestic foundation to build upon as he and chief financial officer Adam Santo attempt to restore FA’s cash position. “Two significant losses, and increasing losses year-on-year, is obviously not a situation that is sustainable or acceptable,” Kugeler said. Martin Kugeler and Heather Garriock. Getty Images for Football Australia Kugeler, who began as FA chief executive in February, said it would be “unfair” to criticise the administrators who came before him, but conceded there had been a collective failure on football’s part to turn those opportunities into financial outcomes. “Have we capitalised, as Football Australia, the maximum out of that tournament? We’ll probably agree on this call that we haven’t,” he said.



Kugeler declined to answer a question as to whether he was aware of the magnitude of FA’s issues before he took the job. Workers at FA were being called into meetings on Tuesday to learn their fates. Kugeler said redundancies were a last resort, and a decision that was taken only after reductions in spending on travel, projects and other external costs. He said the staffing overhaul would reshape FA around “growth and innovation”, with investment planned in digital products, analytics, fan engagement and commercial strategy, even as staffing numbers are slashed. “It’s not only a reduction, a redundancy. It’s also investing in new roles for our forward strategy,” he said. “We have got an exciting time ahead of us with the women’s World Cup in Brazil, but then also with the [2028] Olympics … obviously the Socceroos this year, our national teams will have exposure on the global stage, and that’s where we need to capitalise better than in the past.”



Related Article Scottish Premiership Broken Hearts: Socceroo left in tears as Scottish title bid ends in ‘shameful scenes’ Kugeler said the job cuts would not directly impact the Socceroos’ preparations for the World Cup, their search for new heads of men’s and women’s football who would sit underneath Heather Garriock, FA’s deputy chief executive and executive director of football – nor would it hamper their negotiations with Socceroos coach Tony Popovic over a new contract. Kugeler confirmed publicly for the first time that FA’s preference is to retain Popovic, presumably over the next four-year World Cup cycle. “The discussions are ongoing with his agent,” he said. “He’s obviously focusing on the preparation of the World Cup. We would like Tony Popovic to continue as Socceroos coach. I’ve got the impression that he would like to continue as Socceroos coach.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: The enormous cost of  underfunding schools
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters The enormous cost of underfunding schools May 19, 2026 — 7:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. Photo: Matt Golding STATE OF EDUCATION The NAPLAN analysis (“School tests reveal poor students are years behind”, 19/5) reveals how badly our public education is failing students and Australia generally. The cost of underfunding our public education is enormous. Young people who are failing create chaos in the classroom, in their own and their families’ lives and, in some cases, in our communities. So what is the short-sighted solution we are given? More police and more prisons. Every Australian will benefit if every child is provided with the educational support to achieve. Invest in our children and invest in the prosperity of all Australians.

Judy Kevill, Ringwood Remove private school aid for a ‘fair go’

Australians generally pride themselves as a country of “a fair go”, but not it seems where your postcode and parents’ income and qualifications really count. If we really are progressive and take inequity seriously, then we must remove the funding provided to private schools and instead fully support the public system.

Denise Stevens, St Kilda



Governments need to try harder

Sober reading to see such inequality of educational outcomes in Australia (“School tests reveal poor students are years behind”, 19/5). We have known about this trend for years, mainly caused by inadequate funding of state education and unnecessary federal funding of private schools. We also read of government money for affordable housing being misdirected (“Analysis pans ‘affordable’ housing”, 19/5). People who need social housing are missing out. This compounds educational disadvantage.

Our prime minister said, “no one would be left behind”. People were and they still are. Governments need to try harder, not just by increasing funding where it will be effective, but also by oversight of existing funding and how it is spent. Why are we not demanding better?

Jan Marshall, Brighton AI taking over the classroom

As a retired teacher, I was horrified by the distress of a family member relating to me how the government high school where she teaches permits staff organising the curriculum and student assessments to use AI to facilitate their work. The result is a shambolic interpretation of the curriculum needs of the school and non-personal assessment of students’ progress. Young teachers have no problem with using AI, apparently. To traditionally trained senior staff, this abrogation of duties is confronting and extremely stressful to the point where they are leaving government schools in droves. Is the state minister for education across all this?

My relative also tells me she is struggling to teach year 7 students who have reached high school with shockingly poor handwriting, reading and writing skills … obviously, not properly taught in primary schools any more.

Kaye Kibblewhite, Frankston South When patriotism falls by the wayside

I asked an 18-year-old male what the word, “patriotism”, meant. He had no idea, despite being a university student. It suggests that basic values are no longer taught in our public education system.

Heaven help this country when our national identity is not respected and celebrated in our schools.

Michael Gamble, Belmont The results speak for themselves

It comes as no surprise to teachers and other educators that students in schools that offer free lunches, small class teaching and other benefits such as affordable uniforms and free medical checks show better academic results than students in rundown, under-resourced schools.

Instead of spending hundreds of thousands of dollars on NAPLAN and other “indicators” of need, why not spend the money on making sure all government schools are fully equipped and are places where all students are encouraged and supported and can feel a sense of pride in their schools?

Cheryl Day, Beaumaris THE FORUM



Budget blow for nature

I was in the emergency department with my son on the night the federal budget was handed down. As I looked after my son, it was the government’s job to make the right decisions for Australians, which includes looking after nature.

Instead, already minuscule nature funding took further hits, including $2.2 billion in cuts to the Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water portfolio, along with 378 staff cuts.

Nature is part of the systems that keep life working, and we rely on it for things like clean water, healthy food, stable weather, and jobs. Nature loss is becoming a real risk to economies and communities, not just ecosystems.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers spoke often about this being a fair intergenerational budget but when our government spends less than 10¢ in every $100 on looking after nature, that means leaving future generations to inherit an environmental and economic debt.

My son was OK that night, but it was enough to make you stop and think about the things that matter, and about the kind of future you’re trying to leave for your kids. Nature underpins that future, and I’m disappointed the government is still failing to see that.

Jody Gunn, CEO, Australian Land Conservation Alliance Time for action is now

Infrastructure Victoria in its Warning Signs report (“Warning on roads, rail and climate toll”, 19/5) details the risks and costs from climate events such as storms, flooding, heat and fires. The worsening environmental, economic and social cost burden on our communities is undeniable. Yet, one wonders what it will take for Australian governments to finally act on these such reports.

Ratepayers and taxpayers cannot carry these risks any longer. It’s time for the big polluters, whose emissions cause the destruction, to pay for it. Now that would be real tax reform!

Brenda Tait, Northcote Busting tax myths

Many myths are regularly promulgated about tax in Australia. We are a “high tax” country relative to others, and we have “high income tax”, they say.

Comparing apples with apples, neither is true. What is true is that most Western countries have an inheritance tax and we don’t.

The OECD average rate is about 15 per cent. France has a 60 per cent inheritance tax!

With all the problems associated with rapidly increasing inequality in our country, an inheritance tax is something we have to consider seriously.

Tim Mahar, Fitzroy North Taylor’s absurd claim

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor’s claim that the new tax on trusts is death tax by stealth is absurd (“Tax scare flimsy, but might stick”, 19/5). The tax will be levied year by year on the trust income, not at the time of death. For far too long, certain members of the community have used family trusts to reduce their contribution to society via fair taxes.

Reg Murray, Glen Iris Wrong on wealth

It is disappointing but not surprising to read multiple correspondents (Letters, 19/5) excusing Labor’s broken promises, categorising older Australians and investors as a self-interested cohort of wealthy people.

Some facts: Most negatively geared property owners have only one or two such assets, are not billionaires, and have earned the money they invested by lawful means through their own work and sound decision-making.

They do this to prepare for a retirement without needing to depend on taxpayer-funded welfare, and to provide for their children on death. To condemn such people as being driven by self-interest to the exclusion of wider society’s interests unfairly demonises this group.

William Vickers, Melbourne



Chalmers misses mark

One must assume that Treasurer Jim Chalmers thinks everyone over 65 with private health cover is wealthy. Not so. Many part-pensioners make sacrifices in order to keep themselves off extraordinarily lengthy public health waiting lists. They are doing the system a favour!

Hearing Chalmers argue that neighbours – a young family and a pensioner couple – should have the same private health rebate is nonsensical. The family has earning capacity and is likely to be healthier.

The private health insurance rebate needs to be means tested. That would be a fair outcome.

Yvonne Trevaskis, Hobart, Tas. Concern over NDIS plan

Let’s look at the real cost of the NDIS. I am the mother of a profoundly disabled son who requires 24-hour care. The NDIS has changed Tom’s life.

Health Minister Mark Butler’s planned removal of up to 160,000 participants from the NDIS and the reduction of many plans from the scheme has many families scared.

Not once have I heard what the NDIS brings into the economy. Every dollar in a participant’s plan generates $2.25 directly into the economy: the therapists who support the participants, the businesses that provide the equipment such as wheelchairs, and most importantly, the support workers. They enable my family to work and for my 21-year-old son to be supported safely and with the respect that he deserves.

Butler’s proposed bill risks damaging the original intent of the NDIS which was to provide participants with reasonable and necessary supports so they can live a life with respect and dignity.

Sarah Alcock, North Balwyn Related Article Note From The Editor How The Age chooses which letters to publish Allan must resign

It seems like hardly a week goes by that Premier Jacinta Allan is yet again caught on the back foot explaining aspects of the Big Build and purported corruption. We learn that more than $6 million was claimed for work that was never carried out (“Police to probe Metro tunnel rort”, 18/5). In the past two weeks, we learnt of extraordinary lapses of probity within the hiring system of female workers. On top of this, the extension of the lottery licence was carried through in secrecy.

I think the electorate by now sees that the situation in Victoria and its massive debt cannot be tolerated much longer and the premier must do the only decent thing and resign.

Tony Davidson, Glen Waverley Opposition missing

On the Big Build’s rorts and scandals, your correspondent asks, “Where is the accountability?” (Letters, 17/5) It should also be asked, “Where was the opposition?” The Westminster system relies on the opposition scrutinising the work of government. Yet, these scandals have been uncovered by the excellent work of Nick McKenzie and others from The Age, and there have been no consequences for politicians or bureaucrats. It beggars belief that a state can be run this way.

Barbara Chapman, South Yarra



Smoke signals

While high tobacco excise has undoubtedly fuelled the illegal cigarette market, it does not necessarily follow that reducing the excise on legal cigarettes will reduce or slow the black market (“Cut tobacco excise to slow black market: doctor”, 18/5). Currently, legal cigarettes retail for about $50 a packet compared with $15-$20 a packet for illegal cigarettes. Reducing the price of legal cigarettes to about $30 a pack, as proposed, still leaves illegal cigarettes significantly cheaper.

A reduction in the price of legal cigarettes also sends the wrong signal to existing and potential smokers.

James Proctor, Brown Hill Tobacco issues

The black market for tobacco has reduced tax revenue. But if the objective of high tobacco taxes is to discourage smoking, ultimate success will see no revenue raised.

People on Centrelink benefits assessed as addicted by their doctors could be given access to untaxed tobacco and be encouraged to switch to legal vaping and/or quit. Addicts not on benefits could be given access to affordable tobacco if they participate in quit programs.

In order not to encourage new smokers, a registered addict scheme would be limited to current tobacco addicts.

Andrew Liston, Pascoe Vale Dirty creatures

Exclusive Brethren would have a fit wandering this area to witness people who worship dogs (“Secret sect pet purge sparks new cull fears”, 16/5). And the brethren are quite right – they are dirty and demanding creatures with appalling table manners. They’ll dribble water across the floor after a drink, make the odd awful smell, and roll in or eat things truly disgusting. They’ll hog children’s beds while radiating concepts of “inclusion and equity”. Yet given a choice between instruction from a bunch of older male leaders of a secretive religious sect and rearranging three letters, I think we’ll keep faith with “Devotion to Dog”.

Ronald Elliott, Sandringham Impatient Blues

At 96 years of age, this is the first letter I have ever written to The Age, but as a keen follower of the AFL, I felt compelled to say something. Like many supporters, I have watched with growing sadness the constant turnover of coaches at the Carlton Football Club. Five coaches in 10 years – including interim appointments – is an extraordinary number for any club, particularly one that has struggled so greatly on the field.

Football clubs speak often about patience and long-term planning, yet Carlton’s treatment of coaches has appeared anything but patient. Supporters understand that success cannot happen overnight, but stability, encouragement and faith in leadership surely matters just as much as talent on the field.

Bridget McNamara, Shepparton Hit to hip pocket

On what planet does one can of draught beer and one bottle of still water cost $17.40? Planet Earth, at the Melbourne Cricket Club Express. To quote the MCC website, MCC Express “enhances the fan experience by enabling checkout-free shopping using AI, computer vision, and sensor fusion”. Fans can buy their food and beverages “faster than ever before”. Doesn’t that make you feel good? At a price!

Bill Healy, Kew



AND ANOTHER THING ... Money

As soon as Angus Taylor mentions the words “death taxes”, he loses all credibility – not that he had much anyway, after his preference deals with One Nation.

Philip West, Jan Juc Photo: Matt Golding Given the predicted early demise of the Liberal Party, its concerns about death taxes are understandable.

Peter Gerrand, West Melbourne Pauline Hanson thinks Labor’s budget is “communism redistributing wealth”. So ... Pauline wants her followers to be happy with what they’ve got. Or, in many cases, what they haven’t got.

Scott Lowe, South Melbourne



The budget’s new “death tax” on testamentary trusts will have lawyers and accountants saying to their clients: “If you can just arrange to die before July 1, 2028, you’ll have nothing to worry about ... literally!”

Henry Kalus, Southbank Wait for the next version of Mediscare from the ALP, usually when they get edgy.

Robert Wilson, Jan Juc Victoria

Jeff Kennett does need a statue! His legacy is everywhere: high energy prices, fewer nurses, diluted and privatised public services.

George Reed, Wheelers Hill, Myki readers beep when the user touches their card on or off. Perhaps a “ca-ching” sound effect should be used instead.

Ross McPhee, Seaford As much as I enjoyed reading Peter Mattessi’s article on Life in the Burbs (19/5), when did East Brunswick become Brunswick East?

Anne Brennan, Creswick



Your correspondent says, “Sydneysiders wear swimmers. Victorians wear bathers” (Letters, 19/5). Personally, as a Victorian, I’ve always worn togs.

Michelle Goldsmith, Eaglehawk Furthermore

I assume the umpires will also be wearing black and white for the Collingwood v West Coast match on Saturday?

Bob Speed, Trafalgar Finally

Could we (and the rest of the world) have a Trump-free day, please? Better still, a Trump-free decade.

Warwick Spinaze, Rosebud Related Article Analysis

Auctions Why the auction market just dropped even further, but not everywhere

World.title: The Brisbane creeks with 4000 microplastics in just a kilo of sludge
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPollution The Brisbane creeks with 4000 microplastics in just a kilo of sludge Julius Dennis May 19, 2026 — 7:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

For every kilogram of sediment in two Brisbane creeks, there are more than 4000 tiny pieces of potentially harmful plastic, a new study has found. Queensland University of Technology researchers dredged sludge from Kedron Brook, Enoggera and Bulimba creeks four times over a year in 2024, with roughly 4400 plastic particles found in one kilogram of Kedron Brook’s sediment. Approximately 4100 particles were found in the same amount of Bulimba Creek’s mud, while Enoggera was the cleanest of the three, with 2800 pieces of plastic per kilogram. Heshani Mudalige uses a van veen grab sampler to test the sediment. QUT Microplastics are ubiquitous and can be found in water, earth and in the air. As a result, the broken down plastics have been discovered in every human tissue type, and while the health threats are not fully understood, it has been linked to colon and lung cancer.



PhD candidate Heshani Mudalige said the amount of plastics found in the three Brisbane creeks depended on the gradient, the seasons, and where the creek flowed. “Kedron Brook’s microplastic load is strongly influenced by its running through commercial and industrial areas, including the Brisbane Airport precinct,” she said, noting that the creek’s highest load was in March following heavy summer rains. Kedron Brook runs through Brisbane’s inner-north. Brisbane City Council Mudalige said impervious areas in the Kedron catchment likely brought more microplastics into the creek. She said Enoggera likely had the lowest load because the creek’s flow was regulated by the dam.



Mudalige said 2021 research on the Brisbane River had found about 500 items of plastic per kilo of sediment. Editor's pick Health ‘One of the great human crises’: Warning after microplastics linked to lung, colon cancer She said it was the first time Kedron Brook sediment had been tested for microplastics. Associate Professor Prasanna Egodawatta said the study would fuel future research into how microplastics moved through Brisbane’s urban water systems. “This study is a first step towards quantifying land-based microplastic inputs to Moreton Bay via the stormwater pathway,” Egodawatta said.



While the three creeks do not flow into water treatment plants that could lead to human consumption, Mudalige said the plastics could still pose a danger if they reached the sea. The findings of the QUT research were published in the journal Environmental Pollution. Mudalige is also working on tracking the amount of PFAS “forever chemicals” and heavy metals in the three creeks, with papers to be published in the near future.
